quote: Tversky and Kahneman recorded the estimates of subjects who saw the Wheel of Fortune showing various numbers.
content: The rigged wheel is a fair correction, though a harmless one: the essay reports only the 10 and 65 conditions. The claim that adjustment had been "abandoned" is wrong. Epley and Gilovich showed that the two mechanisms split by the source of the anchor. Anchors the experimenter supplies work mainly through selective accessibility. Anchors the subject generates, such as the first partial product of a multiplication, work through adjustment that stops too early at the first plausible value (Epley & Gilovich 2001; Epley & Gilovich 2006). The essay's second demonstration, 1 × 2 × … × 8 against 8 × 7 × … × 1, is a self-generated anchor, and the essay also cites Strack & Mussweiler, the source of the accessibility account. It covers both mechanisms and uses each where it applies.

quote: try also to think of an anchor in the opposite direction—an anchor that is clearly too small or too large, instead of too large or too small—and dwell on it briefly
content: The procedure that works is the one the essay prescribes, and it was published before the essay was written. Fable counts this as a rarity in the book, but it is the sequence's method: a specific procedure aimed at the bias's mechanism, preceded by noticing that the bias is operating. Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer had the experimenter prompt the correction. Outside the laboratory nobody prompts it, which is why the essay pairs the procedure with "watch yourself thinking, and try to notice when you are adjusting a figure." Noticing is the trigger, and the opposite anchor is the fix. The essay also reports honestly that its first suggestion is insufficient ("subjects instructed to avoid anchoring still seem to do so"). That is an essay following its evidence.
